text:
In day-to-day lab talk an organic chemist commonly checks reaction progress or the ease of a purification by running a thin-layer chromatography (TLC) plate.  
If two components have very similar polarities they travel the plate the same distance and give coincident (overlapping) spots. When visualised, the two spots appear to lie “right on top of each other.” The same wording is also used when compounds co-elute during column chromatography: if their polarities are too similar, they come off the column together and the chemist will say they are “on top of each other.”

The expression is not normally used for

• boiling-point similarity (one would say the bps are “too close”),  
• optical rotation (irrelevant to routine separations), or  
• specific non-covalent self-association (one would mention aggregation or dimerisation).

Thus the complaint most naturally refers to the compounds having nearly the same polarity, making chromatographic separation impossible.

Answer: D
